title: MPLS Label Stack Encoding
subtitle: The 32-bit label stack entry that lets routers forward by label instead of address.
summary: RFC 3032 defines how MPLS labels are attached to a packet. Labels form a stack of 4-octet entries placed between the data link header and the network layer header. Each entry carries a 20-bit label, a 3-bit experimental field, a bottom-of-stack bit and an 8-bit TTL. The RFC also sets the rules for TTL handling, oversize packets and reserved labels, and defines encodings for PPP and Ethernet.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3032 defines how MPLS labels are attached to a packet. Labels form a stack of 4-byte entries placed between the data link header and the network layer header. Each entry holds a 20-bit label, a 3-bit experimental field, a bottom-of-stack bit and an 8-bit TTL. The RFC also sets rules for TTL handling, oversize packets and reserved labels, and defines encodings for PPP and Ethernet.

tldr.problem: MPLS routers forward by label, but labels need a standard on-the-wire encoding for each kind of link.
tldr.mechanism: A stack of 4-octet entries (20-bit label, 3-bit Exp, 1-bit S, 8-bit TTL) sits after the data link header and before the network layer packet, with rules for TTL, reserved labels and oversize packets.
tldr.outcome: It is the basic header of every MPLS packet on Ethernet and PPP links, which is why later RFCs update it rather than replace it.

today: This is the header on the wire in MPLS networks, widely used by service providers for VPNs and traffic engineering. Packet analyzers such as Wireshark decode it, and Ethernet frames with EtherType 0x8847 are MPLS unicast. The spec has been updated many times by RFCs including 3270, 3443, 4182, 5462, 7274 and 9017.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) forwards packets by looking up a short label instead of a full network-layer address. The architecture itself is described in RFC 3031. This document answers a narrower question: how are the labels physically written onto a packet so that a Label Switching Router (LSR) can send it over a link?

The RFC defines the label stack, a sequence of 4-octet entries placed after the data link header and before the network layer header, and the rules for handling the fields in each entry. It specifies encodings for PPP and LAN links, and says the same encoding may suit other links. Some switching hardware, such as ATM switches, may encode the top one or two entries differently, but any additional entries MUST use this encoding.

Because MPLS is independent of the network layer, most rules are protocol-independent. Only a few, such as TTL handling and oversize packets, differ, and the RFC spells those out for IPv4 and IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS forwards packets by looking up a short label instead of a full network address. This RFC defines how labels are written onto a packet so that a Label Switching Router (LSR) can send it over a link. It specifies the label stack, the rules for its fields, and encodings for PPP and LAN links. Because MPLS is independent of the network layer, only a few rules, such as TTL handling, differ for IPv4 and IPv6.

sections.title: The Label Stack Entry
sections.content:
Each label stack entry is 4 octets (32 bits) with four fields. The Label is 20 bits and is what routers look up. The Exp field is 3 bits, reserved for experimental use. The S bit is 1 bit and is set to one on the last entry (the bottom of the stack) and zero on all the others. The TTL is 8 bits.

The top of the stack appears earliest in the packet and the bottom latest. The network layer packet follows immediately after the entry that has S set. When a labeled packet arrives, the top label is looked up, and the lookup yields the next hop and an operation on the stack: replace the top entry, pop it, or replace it and then push one or more additional entries.

The 3-bit field is called Exp in this RFC. RFC 5462 later renamed it the "Traffic Class" field, and RFC 3270 gave it a role in differentiated services. The bit layout did not change.
sections.plainLanguage: Each label stack entry is 4 bytes: a 20-bit label that routers look up, a 3-bit Exp field for experimental use, a 1-bit S flag set only on the last entry, and an 8-bit TTL. The top of the stack comes first in the packet. The lookup on the top label gives the next hop and an operation: replace, pop, or replace and push more entries.

sections.title: Reserved Label Values
sections.content:
Label values 0 through 15 are special. The RFC defines the first four and reserves the rest.

0: IPv4 Explicit NULL
Only legal at the bottom of the stack. Pop the stack, then forward based on the IPv4 header.
1: Router Alert
Legal anywhere except the bottom. The packet is delivered to a local software module; forwarding is decided by the label beneath it. If forwarded, the label should be pushed back first.
2: IPv6 Explicit NULL
Only legal at the bottom. Pop, then forward based on the IPv6 header.
3: Implicit NULL
A label an LSR may assign and distribute but which never appears in the encapsulation. If the new label would be Implicit NULL, the LSR pops instead of replacing.

Values 4 to 15 are reserved; section 6 says IANA may assign them based on IETF Consensus. Later RFCs updated this area, including RFC 4182, which removed the restriction on where Explicit NULL may appear, and RFC 7274, which covers allocating and retiring special-purpose labels.
sections.plainLanguage: Label values 0 to 15 are special. The RFC defines the first four. 0 is IPv4 Explicit NULL, and 2 is IPv6 Explicit NULL. Both are only valid at the bottom of the stack, and the router pops the stack and forwards by the IP header. 1 is Router Alert, which sends the packet to a local software module. 3 is Implicit NULL, which tells the router to pop instead of replace. Values 4 to 15 are reserved.

sections.title: Network Protocol and ICMP
sections.content:
The label stack has no field that says what protocol is inside. So when the last label is popped, the LSR must already know the network layer protocol, and that must be inferable from the label popped at the bottom, possibly together with the network layer header itself. Hence any label first pushed onto a packet must be used only for one network protocol, or only for a set of protocols that can be told apart by inspecting the header. The same must hold whenever that label is replaced. If every label in the stack meets this criterion, even intermediate routers can produce protocol-specific errors. A packet that cannot be forwarded and whose protocol cannot be identified MUST be silently discarded.

Sending an ICMP message back for a labeled IP packet requires that the LSR can tell it is IP and can route to the source address. Inside a transit domain whose interior routers do not know external routes, the RFC suggests ASBRs inject a default route into the IGP. When private addresses are tunneled through a public backbone, it suggests copying the label stack onto the ICMP message and label-switching it onward, so it reaches a router that can route it back to the source.
sections.plainLanguage: The label stack does not say which protocol is inside. When the last label is popped, the router must already know the protocol, so a label may be used only for one protocol, or for protocols that can be told apart by their headers. A packet that cannot be forwarded and whose protocol is unknown must be silently discarded. Returning ICMP errors can need extra measures, such as a default route.

sections.title: Time to Live Processing
sections.content:
The TTL field stops packets from circulating forever. The "incoming TTL" is the TTL of the top entry on receipt. The "outgoing TTL" is the larger of (incoming TTL minus one) and zero. If the outgoing TTL is 0, the packet MUST NOT be forwarded, and the label stack must not be stripped to forward it as unlabeled; it may be discarded or passed to the ordinary network layer for error handling such as an ICMP message. When forwarded, the top entry's TTL MUST be set to the outgoing TTL.

For IP, the TTL of the entry is set to the IP TTL (the IPv4 TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit) when a packet is first labeled. When the last label is popped, the IP TTL SHOULD be replaced with the outgoing TTL, which in IPv4 also requires a header checksum update. The RFC notes that some administrators prefer to decrement the IP TTL by one across the whole MPLS domain instead of by the number of hops. Only the top entry's TTL has any significance; others are ignored.

The outgoing TTL depends only on the incoming TTL, regardless of how many labels are pushed or popped along the way. RFC 3443 later updated these rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The TTL field stops packets from circulating forever. The outgoing TTL is the incoming TTL minus one, but never below zero. If it is 0, the packet must not be forwarded. When a packet is first labeled, the entry's TTL is copied from the IP TTL, and the IP TTL may be updated when the last label is popped. Only the top entry's TTL matters.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Path MTU
sections.content:
Pushing labels grows a packet by 4 bytes per label, so a 1500-byte frame payload that gets another label needs 1504 bytes. The RFC defines the Conventional Maximum Frame Payload Size (1500 bytes for Ethernet) and the True Maximum, which on Ethernet is believed to be 4-8 bytes larger, and whose use depends on the equipment.

An LSR SHOULD support a configurable "Maximum Initially Labeled IP Datagram Size". If set above zero, an unlabeled datagram without the DF bit that exceeds it is fragmented before labeling. The RFC's example is 1488, so that even three pushed labels still fit in 1500 bytes.

A labeled datagram that exceeds the True Maximum MUST be treated as too big; one that exceeds only the Conventional Maximum MAY be. For too-big IPv4 datagrams with DF set, the LSR strips the labels, drops the datagram, and sends ICMP Destination Unreachable ("Fragmentation Required and DF Set") with a Next-Hop MTU equal to the effective maximum minus N, where N is 4 times the number of entries. Without DF, it fragments with each fragment at least N bytes smaller than the effective maximum and relabels each. For IPv6, it sends a Packet Too Big message and discards, unless the datagram is 1280 bytes or less and has a fragment header, in which case it fragments.
sections.plainLanguage: Each label adds 4 bytes to a packet, so a full-size Ethernet payload of 1500 bytes may no longer fit. An LSR should support a configurable maximum size for unlabeled datagrams, set low enough to leave room for labels. A labeled datagram that is too big is handled differently by IP version. For IPv4, if the DF bit is set, it is dropped and an ICMP error is sent. Otherwise it is fragmented. For IPv6, a Packet Too Big message is sent.

sections.title: Carrying Labels on PPP and LANs
sections.content:
On PPP links, labeled packets travel only after PPP reaches the Network-Layer Protocol phase and the MPLS Control Protocol (MPLSCP) reaches the Opened state. MPLSCP works exactly like LCP with a few exceptions: its packets use PPP protocol type hex 8281, only Codes 1 through 7 are used, and it has no configuration options. Each PPP frame carries exactly one labeled packet, with PPP protocol hex 0281 for MPLS unicast or hex 0283 for MPLS multicast.

On LAN media each frame carries exactly one labeled packet. The label stack entries follow any data link headers, including 802.1Q headers, and precede the network layer header. EtherType hex 8847 means MPLS unicast and hex 8848 means MPLS multicast. Both values work with either Ethernet or 802.3 LLC/SNAP encapsulation; choosing between them is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: On PPP links, labeled packets travel only after the MPLS Control Protocol (MPLSCP) reaches the Opened state. Each PPP frame carries one labeled packet, with PPP protocol 0281 for unicast or 0283 for multicast. On LANs, label entries follow the data link headers, and EtherType 8847 means MPLS unicast while 8848 means MPLS multicast.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Label values 0 to 15 have special meaning as specified here or as later assigned by IANA. Values 0 to 3 are defined in this document, and 4 to 15 may be assigned by IANA based on IETF Consensus.

The RFC says the encoding raises no security issues beyond those already in the MPLS architecture or the network layer protocol inside it, and it points out two inherited concerns. First, routers whose security checks assume the network layer header sits at a fixed offset from the data link header will not work, because the label stack makes that offset variable. Second, a label means something only through agreement between the router that writes it and the one that reads it, and the stack does not reveal who wrote a label. If labeled packets are accepted from untrusted sources, packets may be routed illegitimately.

In practice this means MPLS networks must not accept labeled packets from untrusted neighbors.
sections.plainLanguage: Label values 0 to 3 are defined here, and IANA may assign 4 to 15 by IETF consensus. The encoding adds no security issues beyond those of MPLS and the protocol inside it. Security checks that expect a fixed header position will break, and a label has meaning only by agreement between the routers that write and read it. MPLS networks must therefore not accept labeled packets from untrusted neighbors.
